label: GPT-6 Luna
output:
**Subject: Cup Day, the Coolroom and Your Delicate London Constitution**

Dear Jonno,

You keep asking what happened with the coolroom on Cup Day, so here it is in one convenient blog post. You can stop messaging me “but what actually happened?” like you’re conducting an inquiry from your little London flat.

The compressor packed it in overnight on Monday. We found out at 6.40 on Tuesday morning, Cup Day, when I looked at the thermometer and it said **11 degrees**.

Eleven.

That’s not a coolroom. That’s a suspiciously cold bedroom.

We had 140 booked for lunch: set menu, three courses, the whole Cup Day circus. Raff was away, so it was me in charge. Phil, the owner, gave me the sort of detailed operational plan you’d expect from a man who had just heard there was a problem and was hoping it might resolve itself.

“Just make it work, mate.”

Cheers, Phil. I’ll add that to the run sheet under *contingency planning*.

The fridge guy, Wally from Coldline, couldn’t get to us until Wednesday. The part had to come from Sydney, which is a nice way of saying: “You’re on your own, champ.”

So we started moving food wherever we could find cold space. Two undercounters. The bar fridge. Marta next door let us use half her walk-in, which was generous of her and also, as it turns out, not free. She’s charging us in croissant credit. I now owe her roughly three weeks of staff meal, and possibly a small percentage of the business.

We still lost about $1,800 worth of stock, mostly dairy and the duck legs. Not ideal. The duck legs had a better Cup Day than I did: they got to lie around all morning while I tried to work out what could be saved, what had to go and whether a bar fridge could somehow develop the capacity of a commercial coolroom through sheer force of will.

It cannot. I checked.

Then came the beef shin. Benny and I had to get about 30 kilos down the laneway on a milk-crate trolley, in the rain. One of the wheels fell off halfway along, because apparently even the trolley had decided it wasn’t getting paid enough for this.

So there we were, pushing a wobbling crate of beef through the wet laneway like a very grim parade float. I’m sure it was a beautiful sight. A real Melbourne Cup moment.

Kev, meanwhile, took the old esky to the servo and filled it with ice. Fourteen bags. The servo guy asked if we were having a party, which I thought was a fair question given Kev looked like he was stocking up for a very specific, very cold emergency party.

By service, we’d rearranged half the kitchen, borrowed a walk-in, iced an esky, lost a trolley wheel and accepted that the menu was now more of a suggestion. You would have absolutely lost your mind.

At 12.15, we had to 86 the panna cotta. So dessert became “affogato with whatever”. And for some reason, people loved it more. Maybe they could sense the desperation and wanted to reward us. Maybe “whatever” is the secret ingredient we’ve been missing. I’m not changing the menu, though. Phil will start calling it a plan.

One lady on table 9 saw Benny and me hauling the beef through the laneway and asked if it was “free range from the laneway”.

Honestly, fair enough. She’d seen the supply chain with her own eyes.

And because the universe has a sense of humour, my horse in the sweep was called **Ice Cold Lad**. He came second last. Even the horse with the cold-themed name couldn’t come through for me. You spend all day trying to keep food cold, then your horse named Ice Cold Lad finishes nearly last. There’s a punchline in there somewhere, but I was too busy trying to find room for dairy.

Here’s the thing, though: it was probably the best service we did all year.

Everyone was locked in. No one panicked, or at least no one panicked where the guests could see. The team just kept working out the next thing that needed doing, then doing it. The kitchen ran on bar fridges and spite, as kitchens so often do. We got 140 people fed, the room was full, the food went out and somehow dessert was a hit despite being invented at short notice.

Not bad for a day that started with an 11-degree coolroom and a management plan of “just make it work, mate”.

So that’s the story. Nothing glamorous. A broken compressor, a lot of rearranging, some expensive dairy, one disabled trolley and a dessert called “whatever”. We got through it, and it’s funny now that I’m not standing in a wet laneway trying to stop 30 kilos of beef shin escaping downhill.

You would’ve hated every second. You’d have been pacing around going, “What do you mean the part’s coming from Sydney?” and “Where are we putting the duck?” and “Is that really the best trolley we’ve got?” Then you’d have eaten the affogato and claimed it was the best dessert you’d ever had.

London’s made you soft, Jonno. You’re probably wearing a scarf indoors and asking if the pub has oat milk. Come home ya flog.
